## Variational Inference

When exact inference is intractable, variational inference allows for approximations [@jordan_introduction_1999; @blei_variational_2017]. The idea is to approximate the true posterior $p(\vz \mid \vy)$ with a simpler, tractable distribution $q(\vz)$, which is chosen to minimise the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between $q$ and $p$. For latent variables $\vz$ and observations $\vy$, the log marginal likelihood separates into the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and KL divergence:

$$
\log p(\vy) = \mathcal{L}(q) + \KL(q(\vz) \| p(\vz \mid \vy)),
$$ {#eq-vi_decomposition}

where the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is:

$$
\mathcal{L}(q) = \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log p(\vy, \vz)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log q(\vz)] = \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log p(\vy \mid \vz)] - \KL(q(\vz) \| p(\vz)).
$$ {#eq-elbo}

Since KL divergence is non-negative, $\mathcal{L}(q) \leq \log p(\vy)$ with equality when $q(\vz) = p(\vz \mid \vy)$. Rather than computing the intractable posterior directly, we are able to turn the problem into an optimisation and find the $q$ that maximises the ELBO, which is equivalent to minimising the KL divergence to the true posterior. 

To show @eq-vi_decomposition, start from the definition of KL divergence:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\KL(q \| p) &= \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}\left[\log \frac{q(\vz)}{p(\vz \mid \vy)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log q(\vz)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log p(\vz \mid \vy)] \\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log q(\vz)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(\vz)}[\log p(\vy, \vz)] + \log p(\vy).
\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging this gives @eq-vi_decomposition. As $\KL(q \| p)$ cannot be computed directly, we choose to instead maximise the ELBO, which is equivalent to minimising KL divergence.

The second form @eq-elbo shows the ELBO's structure. The expected log-likelihood $\mathbb{E}_{q}[\log p(\vy \mid \vz)]$ pushes $q$ to concentrate where the data is explained well, while the KL term $\KL(q \| p(\vz))$ pushes $q$ toward the prior, preventing overfitting [@bishop_pattern_2006]. This trade-off mirrors the data-fit versus complexity balance we see in exact Bayesian inference.

For the models in this dissertation, variational inference serves two purposes. Firstly, it allows for scaling to large datasets. Secondly, it allows for handling the hierarchical structure of DGPs where function values at each layer cannot be analytically integrated out which is discussed later (@sec-dgp-variational). The latent variables $\vz$ correspond to function values $\vf$, and the variational distribution is usually chosen to be Gaussian:

$$
q(\vf) = \mathcal{N}(\vf \mid \vm, S),
$$

with variational parameters $\vm \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ (positive definite). This balances how expressive the approximation is, with still staying computationally feasible. The expectations under $q$ can often be computed analytically for standard likelihood functions.

With this Gaussian choice, the KL term has closed form:

$$
\KL(q(\vf) \| p(\vf)) = \frac{1}{2}\left[\tr(K^{-1}S) + \vm^\top K^{-1} \vm - n + \log|K| - \log|S|\right],
$$

where $K$ is the prior covariance. 

Each of these terms have an interpretable role: $\vm^\top K^{-1} \vm$ penalises the variational mean for straying far from zero in units of the prior length-scale; $\tr(K^{-1}S)$ penalises the variational covariance for being larger than the prior; and $\log|K| - \log|S|$ rewards $q$ for being more concentrated than the prior. These together make $q$ pay a KL cost for deviating from the prior, which helps prevent overfitting.

However, optimisation over a full-rank matrix $S \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ still involves $O(n^2)$ parameters, which remains problematic for large $n$.
